question: Describe the full lifecycle of a singleton bean from BeanDefinition to destruction.
answer: The BeanDefinition is registered and BeanFactoryPostProcessors may modify it. The container instantiates the bean, populates properties (dependency injection), invokes Aware callbacks, then BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization, @PostConstruct / InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet / init-method, then postProcessAfterInitialization (where AOP proxies are created). On context close it calls @PreDestroy, DisposableBean.destroy and the destroy-method.

question: How does Spring resolve circular dependencies between singletons, and why does it fail for constructor injection?
answer: For setter/field injection the DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry uses a three-level cache (singletonObjects, earlySingletonObjects, singletonFactories) to expose an early reference to a partially constructed bean; the ObjectFactory in the third level lets SmartInstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor return an early proxy. With constructor injection the instance does not exist yet, so no early reference can be exposed and a BeanCurrentlyInCreationException is thrown. Since Boot 2.6 circular references are disallowed by default.

question: What is the difference between BeanFactoryPostProcessor and BeanPostProcessor? Give a real example of each.
answer: A BeanFactoryPostProcessor operates on bean definitions (metadata) before any bean is instantiated, e.g. PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer resolving placeholders or ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parsing @Configuration classes. A BeanPostProcessor operates on bean instances after instantiation, e.g. AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor performing injection or AbstractAutoProxyCreator wrapping beans in AOP proxies.

question: Explain the difference between @Configuration full mode and @Bean lite mode (proxyBeanMethods=false).
answer: In full mode the @Configuration class is subclassed with CGLIB so calls between @Bean methods are intercepted and return the container-managed singleton. In lite mode (@Component classes or proxyBeanMethods=false) no CGLIB subclass is created, inter-bean method calls are plain Java calls producing new instances, but startup is faster and it is friendly to GraalVM native images. Boot auto-configurations use proxyBeanMethods=false.

question: How do you inject a prototype-scoped bean into a singleton so that a new instance is obtained each time?
answer: Injecting it directly gives a single instance fixed at singleton creation. Options: inject ObjectProvider<T> (or javax/jakarta Provider<T>) and call getObject(); use @Lookup method injection, where Spring overrides an abstract/stub method with CGLIB; or use a scoped proxy (@Scope(value=prototype, proxyMode=TARGET_CLASS)) which delegates every call to a fresh instance.

question: Why does calling a @Transactional or @Cacheable method from another method of the same class not apply the advice?
answer: Spring AOP is proxy-based: the advice lives in the proxy wrapping the bean. A self-invocation uses this, the raw target, bypassing the proxy so no interceptor runs. Fixes: move the method to another bean, inject the bean into itself (self-injection via @Lazy or ObjectProvider), use AopContext.currentProxy() with exposeProxy=true, or switch to AspectJ compile/load-time weaving.

question: When does Spring use a JDK dynamic proxy versus a CGLIB proxy, and what are the consequences?
answer: JDK dynamic proxies implement the target's interfaces and can only be cast to those interfaces; CGLIB generates a subclass and can proxy classes. Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true). CGLIB cannot advise final classes or final/private methods, and the constructor of the subclass may run, while JDK proxies fail if you inject by concrete class.

question: In what order do multiple aspects apply to the same join point, and how do you control it?
answer: Aspects are ordered by @Order or the Ordered interface; lower values have higher precedence. The highest-precedence aspect runs first on the way in and last on the way out (like nested layers). Within one aspect class, advice order since Spring 5.2.7 is @Around, @Before, @After, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing. Without ordering, precedence between aspects is undefined. E.g. @EnableTransactionManagement(order=...) controls where the transaction interceptor sits relative to your aspects.

question: What is the difference between execution(), within(), @annotation() and bean() pointcut designators?
answer: execution() matches method signatures (return type, declaring type, name, parameters). within() matches all join points within given types or packages. @annotation() matches methods carrying a given annotation, while @within() matches types annotated with it. bean() is Spring-specific and matches by bean name pattern. Spring AOP only supports method execution join points.

question: How does Spring create proxies under the hood and when are they applied in the bean lifecycle?
answer: AbstractAutoProxyCreator (e.g. AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator) is a BeanPostProcessor. In postProcessAfterInitialization it finds Advisors whose pointcuts match the bean, and if any match it builds a ProxyFactory that creates a JDK or CGLIB proxy containing an interceptor chain. For early references in circular dependencies it creates the proxy in getEarlyBeanReference instead, so the same proxy is used consistently.

question: Explain REQUIRED, REQUIRES_NEW and NESTED propagation and when you would use each.
answer: REQUIRED joins the current transaction or starts a new one (the default). REQUIRES_NEW suspends the current transaction and starts an independent one with its own commit/rollback, useful for audit logs that must persist even if the outer transaction rolls back. NESTED uses a JDBC savepoint inside the existing transaction so the inner part can roll back alone while an outer rollback still undoes everything; it requires a DataSourceTransactionManager or savepoint support, not JTA.

question: Which exceptions cause rollback by default with @Transactional and how do you change that?
answer: By default only unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and Error) trigger rollback; checked exceptions commit. Use rollbackFor / rollbackForClassName to add checked exceptions and noRollbackFor to exclude runtime ones. Catching an exception inside the transactional method prevents rollback unless you call TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly().

question: What causes UnexpectedRollbackException: Transaction silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only?
answer: An inner method with REQUIRED propagation participated in the outer transaction and threw a runtime exception; the interceptor marked the shared transaction rollback-only. The outer method caught the exception and tried to commit, so the manager rolls back and throws UnexpectedRollbackException. Fix by letting the exception propagate, using REQUIRES_NEW or NESTED for the inner call, or adding noRollbackFor where appropriate.

question: What does readOnly=true actually do in a Spring/Hibernate application?
answer: It is a hint: JpaTransactionManager sets the Hibernate Session flush mode to MANUAL so dirty checking and flushes are skipped, reducing memory and CPU usage; Hibernate can also drop loaded-state snapshots. With JDBC it calls Connection.setReadOnly(true), which some drivers and routing DataSources use to send queries to replicas. It does not by itself prevent writes in every database.

question: How do you perform an action only after a transaction has successfully committed?
answer: Use @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) on an event listener and publish an ApplicationEvent inside the transaction, or register a TransactionSynchronization via TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization and implement afterCommit. This avoids sending emails or messages for data that is later rolled back. Note that code in afterCommit runs outside the committed transaction, so new writes need REQUIRES_NEW.

question: What is the N+1 select problem and what are the ways to solve it with Spring Data JPA?
answer: Loading N parent entities and lazily accessing a collection or association fires one extra query per parent. Solutions: JOIN FETCH in a @Query, @EntityGraph on repository methods, Hibernate @BatchSize or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size to load associations in batches, or DTO projections that select only needed columns. Detect it with SQL logging or Hibernate statistics.

question: Explain the difference between interface-based projections, class-based (DTO) projections and dynamic projections.
answer: Interface projections declare getters; Spring Data creates proxies and closed projections select only matching columns, while open projections with @Value SpEL load full entities. Class-based projections use a DTO constructor (records work) and require explicit constructor expressions in JPQL for @Query. Dynamic projections add a Class<T> type parameter to a repository method so the caller chooses the projection at runtime.

question: How does optimistic locking work with @Version and how do you handle conflicts?
answer: A @Version column is included in the UPDATE where clause and incremented on each change. If another transaction already modified the row, zero rows are updated and Hibernate throws OptimisticLockException, which Spring translates to ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException. Handle it by returning 409 Conflict to clients, or retrying the whole transaction (e.g. with Spring Retry), never retrying inside the same persistence context.

question: What is the difference between save() on a new entity with an assigned id versus a generated id in Spring Data JPA?
answer: SimpleJpaRepository.save calls persist when the entity is new and merge otherwise. Newness is determined by a null id (or version) by default. With assigned ids the entity looks not-new, so Spring issues a SELECT followed by merge, an extra query per save. Implement Persistable<ID> with isNew() or use a @Version field to make Spring call persist directly.

question: Why is spring.jpa.open-in-view considered an anti-pattern and what happens when you disable it?
answer: Open Session in View keeps the EntityManager open for the entire web request, so lazy loading works in controllers and views, but it holds a database connection during rendering, hides N+1 problems and blurs transaction boundaries. Boot logs a warning when it is enabled implicitly. When disabled, accessing lazy associations outside a transaction throws LazyInitializationException, forcing explicit fetch plans or DTO mapping in the service layer.

question: Describe how a request flows through DispatcherServlet in Spring MVC.
answer: The DispatcherServlet asks HandlerMappings for a handler and its interceptor chain, then finds a HandlerAdapter (RequestMappingHandlerAdapter) that resolves arguments via HandlerMethodArgumentResolvers and HttpMessageConverters, invokes the controller and processes the return value with HandlerMethodReturnValueHandlers. Exceptions go through HandlerExceptionResolvers (including @ControllerAdvice). For views a ViewResolver renders the model; for @ResponseBody the converter writes the body directly.

question: How do you implement consistent error responses in a Spring Boot REST API?
answer: Use @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods returning ProblemDetail (RFC 9457) or ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail>; extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler to cover built-in MVC exceptions. Enable spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled for framework errors. Throw ErrorResponseException or custom exceptions implementing ErrorResponse to carry status, title, detail, type and custom properties.

question: When should you choose WebFlux over Spring MVC, and what happens if you call blocking code inside a reactive pipeline?
answer: WebFlux suits high-concurrency IO-bound workloads, streaming and fully non-blocking stacks (R2DBC, reactive clients) running on a small event-loop thread pool. Calling blocking code (JDBC, Thread.sleep) on an event-loop thread starves all requests sharing it. If unavoidable, wrap it with Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()). With Java 21 virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true) MVC handles blocking IO at high concurrency, reducing the need for WebFlux.

question: What is the difference between a Filter, a HandlerInterceptor and a @ControllerAdvice?
answer: A servlet Filter runs in the servlet container before the DispatcherServlet and sees every request, including static resources and errors (used by Spring Security). A HandlerInterceptor runs inside Spring MVC around handler execution with preHandle, postHandle and afterCompletion, and knows which handler was selected. @ControllerAdvice provides cross-cutting exception handling, @ModelAttribute and @InitBinder for controllers, and is not a request interception mechanism.

question: How does content negotiation work and how would you version a REST API in Spring?
answer: Spring chooses a response media type by comparing the Accept header (or configured parameter strategy) with the producible types of the handler and available HttpMessageConverters, returning 406 if none match. Versioning approaches: URI path (/v1/...), request parameter, custom header, or media type (application/vnd.app.v2+json) using produces conditions. Spring Framework 7 adds first-class API versioning support via ApiVersionStrategy and the version attribute on mappings.

question: Explain the Spring Security filter chain architecture.
answer: DelegatingFilterProxy, registered in the servlet container, delegates to the FilterChainProxy bean, which holds one or more SecurityFilterChain beans each matched by a request matcher. The first matching chain runs its ordered security filters, e.g. CsrfFilter, authentication filters, ExceptionTranslationFilter and AuthorizationFilter. Authentication results are stored in the SecurityContextHolder, by default thread-local.

question: How does authentication work internally with AuthenticationManager and AuthenticationProvider?
answer: An authentication filter builds an unauthenticated Authentication token and passes it to the AuthenticationManager, usually ProviderManager. ProviderManager iterates AuthenticationProviders that support the token type, e.g. DaoAuthenticationProvider loads a UserDetails via UserDetailsService and checks the password with a PasswordEncoder. On success it returns an authenticated token with authorities, stored in the SecurityContext; on failure an AuthenticationException is raised.

question: How do you secure a stateless REST API with JWT using Spring Security's resource server support?
answer: Add spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server, set spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri (or jwk-set-uri), and configure http.oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(...)) with SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS. BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter extracts the token, JwtDecoder validates signature, expiry and issuer, and a JwtAuthenticationConverter maps claims such as scope or roles to GrantedAuthorities. CSRF can be disabled for pure token-based APIs.

question: What is the difference between @PreAuthorize, @Secured and URL-based authorization?
answer: URL-based rules in authorizeHttpRequests protect endpoints at the filter level. Method security with @EnableMethodSecurity protects service methods regardless of entry point. @PreAuthorize/@PostAuthorize accept SpEL expressions such as hasRole('ADMIN') or #id == authentication.name, and @PostFilter filters returned collections. @Secured only accepts a list of role names. Method security is proxy-based, so self-invocation bypasses it.

question: When is CSRF protection required and how does Spring Security implement it?
answer: CSRF matters when the browser automatically sends credentials, typically session cookies, so any cookie-based authentication needs it. Spring Security's CsrfFilter requires a token on state-changing requests (POST, PUT, DELETE), stored via a CsrfTokenRepository (HttpSession or CookieCsrfTokenRepository for SPAs), and compares it to a header or form parameter. Since 6.x the token is BREACH-protected with XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler and loaded lazily. Purely stateless bearer-token APIs can disable it.

question: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work internally?
answer: @SpringBootApplication includes @EnableAutoConfiguration, which imports AutoConfigurationImportSelector. It reads candidate classes from META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports, filters them with conditions (@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty) and orders them with @AutoConfiguration(before/after). Auto-configurations are processed after user configuration, so @ConditionalOnMissingBean lets user beans take precedence.

question: How do you debug why an auto-configuration was or was not applied?
answer: Run with --debug or debug=true to print the Condition Evaluation Report (positive and negative matches with reasons). At runtime, the /actuator/conditions endpoint exposes the same report, and /actuator/beans lists created beans. You can exclude auto-configurations with @SpringBootApplication(exclude=...) or spring.autoconfigure.exclude.

question: How would you write your own Spring Boot starter?
answer: Create an autoconfigure module with an @AutoConfiguration class guarded by @ConditionalOnClass and exposing beans with @ConditionalOnMissingBean so users can override them, bind settings with @ConfigurationProperties, and register the class in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports. Add spring-boot-configuration-processor for IDE metadata. A separate starter module only aggregates dependencies. Test with ApplicationContextRunner.

question: Explain the precedence order of externalized configuration sources in Spring Boot.
answer: From highest to lowest (simplified): devtools global settings, test properties, command-line arguments, SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON, servlet init params, JNDI, Java system properties, OS environment variables, random values, profile-specific application-{profile} files outside then inside the jar, plain application files outside then inside the jar, @PropertySource, then default properties. Relaxed binding maps SERVER_PORT to server.port.

question: What is the difference between @ConfigurationProperties and @Value, and why prefer the former?
answer: @ConfigurationProperties binds a hierarchy of properties to a type-safe object (immutable records via constructor binding are supported), supports relaxed binding, JSR-303 validation with @Validated, Duration/DataSize conversion and generates IDE metadata. @Value injects single values with SpEL support but no relaxed binding for complex structures, no validation and scattered keys. Use @ConfigurationProperties for grouped settings and @Value for occasional one-off values.

question: Compare @SpringBootTest, @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest. When would you use each?
answer: @SpringBootTest starts the full application context (optionally a real server with webEnvironment=RANDOM_PORT) for integration tests. @WebMvcTest loads only the MVC slice (controllers, advice, converters, filters) with MockMvc, mocking services with @MockitoBean. @DataJpaTest loads JPA repositories with an embedded database and rolls back each test. Slices start faster and isolate layers; full tests verify wiring.

question: How does Spring's test context caching work and what breaks it?
answer: The TestContext framework caches application contexts keyed by the merged configuration (classes, profiles, properties, context customizers including @MockitoBean definitions). Tests with identical configuration reuse the context, greatly speeding up suites. Different @MockitoBean sets, @TestPropertySource values, active profiles or @DirtiesContext create or evict contexts. Keep configurations uniform, e.g. via shared base classes, to maximise reuse.

question: How do you test against real infrastructure such as PostgreSQL or Kafka in Spring Boot tests?
answer: Use Testcontainers with the JUnit 5 extension: declare a static @Container field and annotate it with @ServiceConnection (Boot 3.1+) so Boot auto-configures connection details, or use @DynamicPropertySource to register URLs. Testcontainers starts real disposable Docker containers, giving production-like behaviour that embedded fakes like H2 cannot guarantee. Boot also supports Testcontainers at development time via TestApplication with SpringApplication.from(...).

question: Explain chunk-oriented processing in Spring Batch and how transactions relate to chunks.
answer: A chunk step reads items one at a time with an ItemReader, transforms them with an optional ItemProcessor, aggregates them until the commit interval (chunk size) and passes the list to an ItemWriter. Each chunk runs in a single transaction; on success the step execution context (e.g. reader position) is committed, enabling restart from the last committed chunk. Returning null from the processor filters an item.

question: How do skip, retry and restart work in Spring Batch fault-tolerant steps?
answer: Calling faultTolerant() on a step enables skip(Exception).skipLimit(n) to skip bad items and retry(Exception).retryLimit(n) for transient errors. On a write failure the chunk is rolled back and items are reprocessed one by one (scanning) to isolate the failing item. SkipListeners record skipped items. Restart relies on the JobRepository: a failed JobExecution with the same identifying JobParameters resumes from the last committed chunk using saved ExecutionContext state; completed instances cannot be rerun with the same parameters.
